title: Gin It Up!

jokes.text: Ben, your heart's in the right place. Your heart and your butt.
jokes.setup: Leslie is told her heart is in the right place, a standard encouraging phrase.
jokes.punchline: She extends the compliment bizarrely to Ben's butt, undercutting the sincerity with absurd affection.
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie Knope warmth weaponized for comedy — she's so earnestly complimentary that she compliments Ben's butt entirely without irony. The non-sequitur extension of the idiom is well-structured and character-specific. The economy is excellent; it lands in five words.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Your heart is really in the right place.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And your butt.

jokes.text: Crap on a turd!
jokes.setup: Leslie is frustrated about running negative ads against her.
jokes.punchline: Her expletive substitute is so absurdly mild and redundant ('crap on a turd') that the frustration reads as both wholesome and flustered.
jokes.explanation: This is extremely Leslie — a character who refuses to swear properly. The redundancy of 'crap on a turd' is the joke; it's already the same thing. Short, punchy, and only works from this specific character.

jokes.text: Care for a 'Recall Knope' gift bag? / Look what they're handing out at elementary schools. / 'I'm Leslie Knope. Tell your parents to recall me.'
jokes.setup: The committee to recall Leslie is described as relentless.
jokes.punchline: They are handing out recall gift bags to children at elementary schools, complete with a Leslie Knope voice recording telling kids to tell their parents to recall her — a grotesque parody of civic electioneering.
jokes.explanation: The escalating absurdity of political campaigning targeting children is a sharp satirical jab. The Leslie Knope voice recorder saying 'Tell your parents to recall me' is a great visual/audio gag that rewards rewatching. Solid political satire with good comedic escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Recall Committee Member
dialogue.line: Here you go kids, take these gift bags home to your parents.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, what's in the gift bags?

dialogue.speaker: Recall Committee Member
dialogue.line: Recall Leslie Knope pamphlets and buttons.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're handing out anti-me propaganda to third graders?

dialogue.speaker: Recall Committee Member
dialogue.line: It's a grassroots campaign.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's a grass-roots campaign using actual grass roots. You're using children!

jokes.text: Leslie's sticker scheme: 'Don't' sticker + '?' sticker to turn 'Recall Knope' into 'Recall Knope? Don't.' — immediately pointed out that putting 'Don't' in front is simpler.
jokes.setup: Leslie unveils an elaborate, proud plan to use 10,000 stickers to reframe recall signs.
jokes.punchline: Ben instantly points out that the order is wrong and 'Don't' should go in front, making the entire scheme needlessly complicated. Leslie immediately concedes.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed bit. Leslie's elaborate, over-invested solution has an immediately obvious flaw that she's too close to see. Ben's deflation is the perfect straight-man beat, and Leslie's instant 'Yep, that's a much better idea' is self-aware and charming. It's well-earned because we've been walked through the whole convoluted plan.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, why didn't I just... do that?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Because you're Leslie Knope.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you're so right. That's the obvious solution. I love it. Everyone, we're doing this instead.

jokes.text: April asking for the question mark stickers to put on stop signs.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if anyone wants leftover question mark stickers.
jokes.punchline: April immediately wants them to deface stop signs with question marks — casually dangerous and entirely on-brand.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly April joke — absurdly dark, completely casual, and absolutely only she would say it. The implication (stop signs becoming 'Stop?') is both funny and alarming. The economy is excellent; it takes three words to deliver.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Can I have the leftover question mark stickers?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Why do you need question mark stickers?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm going to put them on stop signs so they say 'Stop?' You know, to make people question things.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, that could cause accidents.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Parks can only be reserved for witch covens or slip-and-slide competitions.
jokes.setup: A woman (Nadia) comes in to reserve a park for Doctors Without Borders.
jokes.punchline: Tom has apparently instated a policy allowing only witch covens or slip-and-slide competitions — a completely arbitrary and absurd official policy.
jokes.explanation: A good cold-open absurdist gag. The specific pairing of witch covens and slip-and-slide is a funny combination. It doesn't fully pay off but functions as a solid setup for Tom's character in the scene.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, but according to Parks Department Policy 7-B, subsection 12, medical events can only be scheduled during months that contain the letter 'R', and the organizer must be either a licensed physician or a moderately attractive beaver. You're a doctor, so that checks out, but this month is July, which has no R in it.

jokes.text: Nadia claims to be there for slip-and-slide competition, then immediately admits she's not. Tom: 'Why would you even compete in something like that?'
jokes.setup: Nadia tries to go along with the absurd policy to get her park reserved.
jokes.punchline: Tom's immediate pivot to judging the (fake) slip-and-slide competitive spirit ignores the obvious lie and focuses on the absurd premise.
jokes.explanation: A quick funny misdirect — Tom ignores that she obviously lied and instead questions the legitimacy of competitive slip-and-slide. Good escalation of the absurdist premise but not especially memorable.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You have to choose: witch coven or slip-and-slide.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Um... witch coven?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Wrong answer. It's slip-and-slide.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Wait, I was just playing along. I don't actually believe in witches.

jokes.text: Tom tells Nadia that April is joking about him running the Parks Department 'in his home country of Russia.'
jokes.setup: Tom is clearly nervous around Nadia and trying to impress her. April introduces him as running the whole department.
jokes.punchline: April casually tells Nadia that Tom ran Parks in his 'home country of Russia,' completely undermining him. Tom weakly denies it while also pretending to have a British accent.
jokes.explanation: April sabotaging Tom's flirtation by calling him Russian is perfectly on-brand. The setup of Tom trying too hard with a fake British accent makes April's casual misdirection land well.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So if someone were to slip and fall on a slide that wasn't real, would they still get hurt?

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: I'm not going to answer that.

jokes.text: 'How could I be from Russia? Not with this spot-on British accent.'
jokes.setup: April just accused Tom of being Russian. Tom is speaking in a clearly fake British accent he adopted to seem cooler.
jokes.punchline: Tom uses the very fake accent as evidence he can't be Russian — as if the fake British accent is real and settles the matter.
jokes.explanation: Delightfully illogical self-defense. Tom's total commitment to the fake accent as if it were real, and using it as counter-evidence, is a great character-specific comedy beat. The line works both as a joke and as a revealing character moment about Tom's capacity for self-delusion.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're not a doctor, you're a witch doing satanic rituals.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Literally everything is a weapon, son. That folder, in my hands, is far deadlier than this bow in yours.'
jokes.setup: Someone points out Ron probably shouldn't have a weapon (bow) at work.
jokes.punchline: Ron escalates rather than apologizes, asserting that everything is a weapon and that an ordinary folder in his hands is MORE deadly than the bow.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect Ron Swanson line. It is 100% character-integrated — only Ron would say this, only Ron would mean it absolutely sincerely, and only Ron would have a bow at work in the first place. The escalation from 'you shouldn't have a weapon' to 'everything is a weapon and my folder is deadlier' is a masterclass in character comedy. Highly quotable and broadly beloved by the fan base. Justifies the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hello, I'm Tom Haverford, Director of Business and Revenue Optimization for the Parks Department.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I basically run this entire city. Well, the fun parts anyway.

jokes.text: Ben reacts to seeing Ron and Leslie's will: 'You need that many pages to say Give my stuff to my wife?'
jokes.setup: Ben is asked to witness their will and sees how thick the document is.
jokes.punchline: He reduces the entire lengthy legal document to its supposed essence — 'give my stuff to my wife' — implying no will should need to be that long.
jokes.explanation: Solid setup for the Ron will joke that follows. Ben's reductionism is funny but somewhat generic — this could be any character's line. Serves mainly as a straight-man setup.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Tom, I'm going to help you impress Nadia. I'm going to tell her you're a Russian parks administrator.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? No, April, that's insane.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Your name is Tomislav. You ran the parks system in Moscow for twelve years. You're very serious about it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm not doing this.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You also have a scar from a bear attack. It's on your back, so no one can see it, which is why you never mention it.

jokes.text: Ron's will: 'Upon my death, all of my belongings shall transfer to the man or animal who has killed me.'
jokes.setup: Ben points out that Ron's will is a single sentence and suggests it should be more comprehensive.
jokes.punchline: The content of the will — giving everything to whoever kills Ron — is a perfect absurdist one-liner that is both legally insane and entirely consistent with Ron's worldview.
jokes.explanation: An all-time Parks and Recreation joke and one of the best Ron Swanson lines in the series. The content of the will — bequeathing everything to his killer — captures his entire character philosophy in one sentence: strength, danger, dark pragmatism, and complete disregard for conventional society. 'Man or animal' is the perfect escalating detail. It is maximally quotable, absurdist, and yet feels earned because it is so Ron. This is the episode's standout joke and justifies a 9+ easily.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Russian? Me? No, no, no. I'm not Russian. I'm British, mate. Born and raised in London, England.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The name's Tom. Tom Haverford. Very British. Tea and crumpets and all that.

jokes.text: 'What are these weird symbols?' / 'The man who kills me will know.'
jokes.setup: Ron's will is revealed to contain mysterious symbols alongside the text.
jokes.punchline: Ron explains the symbols are only for the intended killer — implying there is a specific destined killer who will understand them. Delivered with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback and escalation to the killer-will joke. The implication that Ron has a specific destined killer in mind who will recognize secret symbols is a phenomenal deepening of the bit. Deadpan delivery makes it land even harder. 'The man who kills me will know' is an extraordinarily quotable standalone line.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A folder would be much deadlier.

jokes.text: The council tables every single one of Leslie's bills and then votes to end the session early so nothing can get done.
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to get actual work done by introducing multiple bills.
jokes.punchline: The opposing council immediately tables everything and then caps it off by voting to end the session early — the logical extreme of obstruction.
jokes.explanation: A solid structural joke about political obstruction taken to its comedic endpoint. The escalation from 'table everything' to 'end the session entirely' is funny. Slightly telegraphed but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: A folder would be deadlier than a bow in my hands.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: ...Yeah, that's fair.

jokes.text: 'Sorry, Knope. We're just looking for any possible way to get you recalled because we don't like you. It's nothing personal.' / 'It absolutely is personal. That is the definition of personal.'
jokes.setup: The council openly admits they're trying to recall Leslie purely because they don't like her.
jokes.punchline: They call it 'nothing personal' — a complete misuse of the phrase — which Leslie immediately and correctly calls out.
jokes.explanation: Sharp structural joke built on the misuse of a cliché. The idiocy of saying 'it's nothing personal' after admitting pure personal dislike is well-observed. Leslie's comeback — 'That is the definition of personal' — is satisfying and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A will? It's simple. You die, your stuff goes to people you like. You don't like them? Burn it.

jokes.text: A tweet has been sent from the Parks and Rec account that is 'quite sexually graphic.'
jokes.setup: A serious work crisis is introduced — a rogue tweet from the department account.
jokes.punchline: The buildup — 'quite sexually graphic' and 'take a look at this' — creates a comedy of anticipation before the actual tweet is revealed.
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the Donna tweet reveal. The anticipatory buildup works but the setup itself isn't the joke — the payoff is in the actual content of the tweet.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've left my entire estate to whoever kills me.

jokes.text: Donna: 'And before you get on my case about those stickers, I already did 'em.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is about to confront Donna about the Twitter scandal.
jokes.punchline: Donna preemptively addresses the sticker situation — implying she also already put the stickers on signs, possibly in the wrong order like April wanted to — getting ahead of multiple potential complaints at once.
jokes.explanation: A nice callback to the sticker subplot. The implication that Donna has already deployed the stickers (possibly incorrectly) while not caring about the much larger Twitter scandal happening in the same breath is good Donna characterization.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What are these symbols?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Only my killer will understand them.

jokes.text: 'See you tonight. Hope you like tongue baths, you big, nasty fireman.' / Then a picture of lips and an eggplant.
jokes.setup: The 'sexually graphic' tweet from the Parks account is finally revealed.
jokes.punchline: The specific language — 'tongue baths, you big, nasty fireman' — is both luridly funny and specific to Donna's established character. The eggplant emoji adds a layer of modern internet humor.
jokes.explanation: An outstanding character-comedy payoff. The tweet is perfectly Donna — dramatic, sensual, and entirely unfiltered. 'You big, nasty fireman' is specific enough to be hilarious. The pivot to clinical emoji description ('a picture of lips and then a picture of an eggplant') makes it even funnier. This is a high-quality cringe-comedy reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't need a lawyer. Lawyers are useless. Doctors are useless. And accountants are useless.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ron, you're literally talking to a lawyer right now.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Present company excepted.

jokes.text: Chris: 'I'm both confused, and if we're being totally honest, a little aroused.'
jokes.setup: The team reacts to Donna's explicit fireman tweet.
jokes.punchline: Chris adds a confessional admission of mild arousal — completely candid, slightly oversharing, and totally honest in the way only Chris can be.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Chris Traeger beat. His unfailing honesty and oversharing are his defining traits, and 'if we're being totally honest, a little aroused' is completely him — earnest, self-aware, slightly inappropriate. The structure of 'confused AND aroused' mirrors his dual reaction well.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Lawyers are one of the three most useless jobs.

dialogue.speaker: Someone
dialogue.line: Your possessions will go to the government.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Well, I want a lawyer.

jokes.text: 'Not to give you too much of a peek into my personal life, but this could have been way worse.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Chris are relieved the tweet was relatively mild.
jokes.punchline: Donna's response implies her private account contains far more explicit content — and she's nonchalant about it.
jokes.explanation: A great Donna line. The casual drop of 'this could have been way worse' implies a depth of explicit content that the audience is left to imagine. The economy is strong and it's 100% character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Council member
dialogue.line: I move to end the session.

dialogue.speaker: Council member
dialogue.line: Second.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, we still have seventeen items on the agenda.

dialogue.speaker: Council member
dialogue.line: Exactly.

jokes.text: Jamm brands the scandal 'Twitter Watergate' and says they're looking for a snappier name.
jokes.setup: A press conference is called over the tweet.
jokes.punchline: Jamm is already calling it 'Twitter Watergate' but openly admits they're still searching for a snappier name — revealing the performative theatrics of political scandal-making.
jokes.explanation: A nice media-satire gag about the construction of political scandals. The self-awareness of naming something 'Watergate' while admitting they want something snappier is a sharp political comedy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Council Member
dialogue.line: It's not personal.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's not personal? That's literally the definition of personal. Personal means it's about a person. You don't like me, the person. That's personal.

jokes.text: Jamm: 'Tongue baths? Eggplants? Firemen? Those men are heroes who deserve respect! 9/11!'
jokes.setup: Jamm is dramatically calling out the content of the tweet.
jokes.punchline: He pivots from shock over the eggplant to a completely unearned invocation of 9/11 as if the tweet is disrespecting first responders — an absurd, opportunistic political non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Jamm moments in the episode. The sudden '9/11!' as a rhetorical non-sequitur perfectly satirizes how politicians weaponize tragedy for unrelated political gain. The rhythm — listing the tweet's contents, then slamming in '9/11!' with no logical bridge — is structurally excellent. Very quotable and reveals Jamm's cynicism perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: But you just said it was personal!

dialogue.speaker: Council Member
dialogue.line: It's not personal, it's just business.

jokes.text: 'This will be blown way out of proportion! You have my word on it!'
jokes.setup: Jamm is theatrically indignant at the press conference.
jokes.punchline: He openly promises to blow the scandal out of proportion — an honest confession of political theater disguised as outrage.
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully honest piece of political satire delivered with total conviction. Jamm accidentally (or not) confessing to his own cynical strategy while framing it as a solemn vow is a tightly structured irony joke.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'm gonna go home and have a drink with a firefighter.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'He is not gonna Sully your name.' / Ben: 'Not on her watch.' / Ann (or Donna): 'No sullying allowed!' / Leslie: 'Guard your buds, 'cause they're about to get nipped!'
jokes.setup: Leslie rallies her team to defend Donna from Jamm.
jokes.punchline: The rallying speeches escalate from sincere ('Not on her watch') to completely off-base ('Guard your buds, cause they're about to get nipped!'), which is a bizarre riff on 'nip it in the bud' that loses the thread entirely.
jokes.explanation: A moderately funny escalation of supportive affirmations that peaks with the 'guard your buds' mangling of the idiom. The joke is in the unraveling of a cliché into something that doesn't quite make sense. Charming but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: There's a peach, an eggplant, a water droplet, and a little skull emoji. The skull emoji is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm not gonna lie, I'm a little turned on right now.

jokes.text: 'Pawnee is like a petri dish of weird diseases. Did you know you have a higher rate of the West Nile virus than the actual Western Nile? Sorry, West Nile, looks like Pawnee wins again.'
jokes.setup: Nadia explains why Doctors Without Borders chose Pawnee.
jokes.punchline: Pawnee has more West Nile virus than the actual Nile River — framed as civic pride ('Pawnee wins again').
jokes.explanation: A strong Pawnee-mythology joke. The running gag of Pawnee being a uniquely diseased and dysfunctional place is extended to an absurd extreme — beating the actual Nile. The 'Pawnee wins again' spin, treating this as civic pride, is a great character/place-comedy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Y'all are overreacting. This is literally the tamest thing I've ever tweeted.

jokes.text: 'What else have you beaten the Western Nile in?' / 'Cricket.'
jokes.setup: Tom asks Nadia to elaborate on Pawnee's dubious 'victories' over the actual Nile region.
jokes.punchline: She says 'Cricket' — which is both a weird disease-adjacent answer and also a sport, creating an ambiguity that's funnier than either reading alone.
jokes.explanation: A quick, compact joke with excellent economy. 'Cricket' is a funny non-answer that works on multiple levels. Not deep, but efficiently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: This Twitter scandal is a disgrace to our city. We need to remember what happened on 9/11.

jokes.text: Tom: 'we will be all set like two biscuits inside a tin' — the fake British accent malfunctioning into a weird idiom.
jokes.setup: Tom is maintaining his fake British accent to impress Nadia.
jokes.punchline: The accent produces a bizarre non-idiomatic phrase ('two biscuits inside a tin') that makes no sense as an expression but sounds vaguely British.
jokes.explanation: Tom's fake British idiom going off the rails is a good character beat. The expression is so non-idiomatic it loops back around to funny. His commitment to the bit in the face of obvious failure is characteristic.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Don't worry, I'm going to blow this completely out of proportion.

jokes.text: April confesses Tom 'panicked' and made himself talk British so he'd 'seem cooler.'
jokes.setup: Tom has been maintaining a fake British accent the whole time.
jokes.punchline: April's deadpan confessional explains what we suspected — it was pure romantic panic.
jokes.explanation: A good talking-head beat that confirms the joke we've been watching. April's clinical assessment of Tom's panic is very her. Functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: We're going to nip this in the bud.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: Yes! And then we'll water it down, let it wilt, and throw it in the compost bin!

jokes.text: Ben: 'I mean, obviously, accountants are a little more bad boy, but uh, there's a respect there.'
jokes.setup: Ben is explaining that he and a lawyer 'speak the same language.'
jokes.punchline: Ben positions accountants as the 'bad boys' of finance professions — a completely delusional claim delivered with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Ben Wyatt moment. His self-image as slightly edgier than lawyers — both being among the least 'bad boy' professions imaginable — is exactly his brand of earnest nerdiness. The casual 'but uh, there's a respect there' adds to the delusion.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: We want to establish a regional office here in Pawnee.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's wonderful! Why Pawnee?

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Pawnee somehow has more West Nile virus than the region it's named after.

jokes.text: Ben introduces the lawyer meeting as Ron doing some 'Good Will Hunting' — a pun on the film and Ron needing to draw up a will.
jokes.setup: Ben is introducing Ron to the lawyer for estate planning.
jokes.punchline: He makes a 'Good Will Hunting' pun — will = legal document + will = good will — and then over-explains it.
jokes.explanation: A decent pun that is immediately undermined by Ben's overeager explanation and the lawyer's flat rejection. The joke is partly in how bad the pun is for the room. Functional but not sharp comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, so Pawnee has the highest disease rate in the state. But look, we're number one at something. We're beating the entire Western Nile region in... in...

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: ...disease rates.

jokes.text: Lawyer Trevor: 'Yes, I understood, Mr. Wyatt. Thank you. As I've said before, I just don't like puns.'
jokes.setup: Ben makes the 'Good Will Hunting' pun and starts to explain it.
jokes.punchline: Trevor cuts him off, revealing he already knows and simply doesn't like puns — implying Ben has done this before.
jokes.explanation: Good deflation beat. Trevor's 'as I've said before' implies a prior history of Ben's puns — adding characterization while executing the anti-comedy of a joke being firmly rejected.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm going to sound very British and sophisticated right now.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's absolutely brilliant, innit? Bob's your uncle, Queen's gambit, fish and chips, Big Ben.

jokes.text: Ron refuses to disclose his assets or where his money is 'hidden, or which precious metals and/or gemstones it may or may not take the form of.'
jokes.setup: The lawyer asks Ron for a standard list of assets and liabilities.
jokes.punchline: Ron refuses, and the refusal reveals that his money is hidden somewhere and exists in the form of precious metals and gemstones — not bank accounts.
jokes.explanation: One of the great Ron Swanson wealth-hiding jokes. The line 'which precious metals and/or gemstones it may or may not take the form of' is structurally brilliant — 'may or may not' is a legal hedge that still reveals everything. It perfectly expands Ron's established character (off-grid, anti-government, gold hoarder) through pure self-contradiction. Highly quotable and strongly character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I mean, compared to lawyers, accountants are the bad boys. We're out here just living on the edge, doing whatever we want. Last week I wore a polo shirt with khakis. A polo shirt!

jokes.text: Trevor: 'I'm gonna say this one last time, Wyatt. Check the accountant crap at the door.' / Ben: 'Yes, sir, I will.' / Ben (confessional): 'Unintentional.'
jokes.setup: Trevor is fed up with Ben's puns.
jokes.punchline: Ben responds with 'Yes, sir, I will' — accidentally making another will pun — and then immediately confesses to camera it was unintentional.
jokes.explanation: The ideal conclusion to the running pun gag. The accidental pun ('I will') is more structurally satisfying than the intentional ones because it shows the universe conspiring against Ben. The confessional 'Unintentional' is perfectly timed and economic — one word, huge laugh. The mockumentary format makes the talking-head confession land brilliantly. This is the best execution of the running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ron, I'd like you to meet our estate planning lawyer.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Pleasure.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I told him about your legal needs. Guess you could say we're hunting for some good will.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's the worst thing I've ever heard.

jokes.text: Jamm announces the hearing's two goals: (1) find out how the tweet happened, and (2) 'turn this whole thing into a media circus.'
jokes.setup: Jamm opens the formal hearing with official-sounding procedural language.
jokes.punchline: He reads goal #2 straight from notes — 'turn this whole thing into a media circus' — as if it were a legitimate governmental objective.
jokes.explanation: Another sharp Jamm political-satire beat, delivered with perfect procedural deadpan. The joke is in how the naked cynicism is presented with bureaucratic formality, as if 'media circus' were a standard item on a hearing agenda.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I guess you could say making a will is all about having the write idea.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: I don't like puns.

jokes.text: Jamm accuses Leslie of 'intracksidence' — not a word.
jokes.setup: Jamm is trying to deliver a formal accusation at the hearing.
jokes.punchline: He uses the word 'intracksidence' — clearly not a real word — and Leslie immediately says 'Not a word.'
jokes.explanation: A good quick joke. Jamm's malapropism/made-up word is a consistent character trait (he's pompous and not particularly intelligent), and Leslie's flat correction is the ideal straight-man response.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: I can't help you without more information.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You just need to have the will to do it.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: Sir, I literally need your will. The legal document.

jokes.text: Leslie's chocolate milk / flip-flop defense: When she was four she thought chocolate milk came from brown cows, then flip-flopped when she learned about chocolate syrup.
jokes.setup: Jamm accuses Leslie of flip-flopping on whether the tweet was from a hacker or an employee.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's defense is a childhood example of updating a belief based on new information — completely valid logically, completely bonkers as a hearing defense.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured Leslie Knope joke. She's completely right (updating beliefs with new information is rational), but her example is so childlike and earnest that it deflates the seriousness of the hearing. It's both absurd and genuinely clever. Very quotable and character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: Ben, stop with the puns! I'm serious.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I know you are. And don't worry - I have the will to stop.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh no... I did it again, didn't I?

jokes.text: Jamm: 'I don't think I'm out of line when I say that this scandal makes Benghazi look like whitewater!'
jokes.setup: Jamm is grandstanding about the severity of the tweet scandal.
jokes.punchline: He invokes two political scandals with zero irony, but gets the scale completely wrong — comparing a spicy tweet to Benghazi AND Whitewater simultaneously, implying the tweet is worse than both.
jokes.explanation: A sharp political satire joke about the inflation of scandal rhetoric. Saying a tweet 'makes Benghazi look like Whitewater' (which was itself heavily politicized) reveals Jamm's complete detachment from perspective. The line is well-structured and very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so what happened was I tweeted about the pothole on Ramsett Street, but then it got retweeted by the bot account, which made it look like I was endorsing the thing about the... the thing... and now everyone thinks I hate... infrastructure? No wait, I LOVE infrastructure. I'm very pro-infrastructure. But the tweet made it sound like I was anti-infrastructure, which is basically anti-Pawnee, which makes me anti-government, which technically makes me a libertarian, and you KNOW how I feel about libertarians!

jokes.text: Jamm: 'Perhaps he or she—' / Other official: '—Or them. It could be a bunch of hot ladies.'
jokes.setup: The council is discussing the unnamed tweeter's identity.
jokes.punchline: Someone suggests the tweeter could be 'a bunch of hot ladies' — an entirely non-sequitur wish-fulfillment suggestion in an official hearing.
jokes.explanation: A quick character joke about the council's incompetence and sexism. The non-sequitur nature of 'a bunch of hot ladies' in an official proceeding lands as absurdist character comedy. Not complex but efficiently delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: As per the municipal code, we need to follow proper protoculation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not a word.

jokes.text: Tom has bought Nadia four bags of coffee beans and a mini espresso machine — having no idea what she wanted.
jokes.setup: Tom is wildly overcompensating in his attempts to impress Nadia.
jokes.punchline: He reveals the escalating gift stack — cappuccino, latte, four bags of beans, AND a mini espresso machine — showing his total inability to calibrate.
jokes.explanation: A fun visual escalation gag. The list builds from reasonable to absurd (a whole espresso machine). Character-specific to Tom, who always overshoots with grand gestures.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: You keep changing your story. First you said one thing, now you're saying another.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Okay, well, when I was a kid, I thought chocolate milk came from brown cows. Then I learned it actually comes from regular cows, and they add chocolate. Did that make me a liar? No. It made me a learner. And that's what I'm doing here — learning and growing.

jokes.text: Tom's British accent is gone; he claims a recent cold affected his voice 'in certain British ways.'
jokes.setup: Nadia notices Tom no longer has the British accent he had earlier.
jokes.punchline: Tom invents the excuse that a cold affected his voice 'in certain British ways' — a transparently absurd explanation delivered with complete commitment.
jokes.explanation: 'In certain British ways' is a brilliantly specific nonsense qualifier that sounds medical while explaining nothing. Tom's earnest commitment to an obviously failing lie is a great character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: This Twitter scandal is just like Watergate, Iran-Contra, and the Monica Lewinsky affair combined.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: But ultimately, it's completely meaningless and nobody cares.

jokes.text: 'Well, that's all there is to that story, so no need for any more questions.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just given a transparently false explanation for the missing accent.
jokes.punchline: He immediately tries to shut down further inquiry with the most suspicious possible deflection.
jokes.explanation: A good short beat — the guilty person trying to end the conversation too quickly. Works as a character moment and decent irony joke. Functional rather than standout.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: We should be inclusive about gender pronouns in this investigation.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, absolutely. She, her, hers... them, they, theirs... and also me with multiple women at the same time.

jokes.text: Nadia: 'You have a cold? Can I feel your glands?' / Tom: 'Sure.' / Nadia: 'Wow, you are wearing a lot of moisturizer on your throat. Best way to prevent crow's neck.' / 'Is this glitter?'
jokes.setup: Nadia, as a doctor, takes Tom's fake cold claim at face value and goes clinical.
jokes.punchline: She finds moisturizer and glitter on his throat — implying Tom has been applying beauty products to maintain the British-person aesthetic or has just been very extra.
jokes.explanation: A wonderful escalating cringe gag. The doctor's professional response to Tom's lie lands her in intimate physical proximity discovering the ridiculous lengths of Tom's vanity. The cascade — moisturizer, then the deadpan 'best way to prevent crow's neck,' then 'Is this glitter?' — is perfectly timed escalation. The glitter is the killer detail.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.line: Wait, where's your British accent? It's completely gone.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, that? Yeah, I caught a cold. It affects your voice in very British ways. The accent just... evaporates. It's science.

jokes.text: Tom's confessional: He's using 'the most powerful weapon I have — bureaucratic incompetence' to keep Nadia in town.
jokes.setup: Tom wants to keep the attractive doctor in Pawnee.
jokes.punchline: His 'most powerful weapon' is deliberately messing up government paperwork — a deeply unflattering self-description that is also entirely believable for a Pawnee government employee.
jokes.explanation: A good Parks and Rec joke about the show's central satirical premise — government inefficiency — being weaponized for romantic purposes. The phrase 'bureaucratic incompetence' as a romantic weapon is inherently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.line: Let me take a look at you.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.line: You don't have a cold. You're wearing moisturizer. A lot of moisturizer.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, wrinkles are a sign of aging, and I'm not getting any younger.

jokes.text: Tom gave Nadia Form 3208 (to lease a hangar at an airport) instead of Form 3248 (to reserve a park). 'I know. It's so crazy, it almost sounds made up.'
jokes.setup: Tom is deliberately messing up Nadia's paperwork to stall her.
jokes.punchline: The wrong form is to lease an airport hangar — a wonderfully random error — and Tom's meta-acknowledgment 'it almost sounds made up' is a perfectly deadpan wink at the audience.
jokes.explanation: The specific wrongness of the form (airport hangar) is funnier than a generic mistake. Tom's self-aware 'it almost sounds made up' is a gentle meta-moment that works because he delivers it with such innocence.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.line: Now there's glitter on his neck too.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's a moisturizer with subtle shimmer. It's for men.

jokes.text: Someone left out a blender, fresh fruits, and rum — 'I guess we gotta, like, make Daiquiris now.'
jokes.setup: Office scene, transition moment.
jokes.punchline: Finding daiquiri ingredients is treated as a binding obligation rather than a choice — 'I guess we gotta.'
jokes.explanation: A brief, functional office gag. The joke is in the passive inevitability — treating daiquiri-making as forced upon them by circumstance. Mild and thin but a quick beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm gonna use government inefficiency as a dating strategy. See, I'll take a girl out on a date, and then I'll say, 'You know what? The government is so inefficient, it takes them six months to process a marriage license.' She'll be like, 'That's crazy!' And I'll be like, 'Yeah, so we might as well just skip all that and go straight to my apartment.' It's foolproof.

jokes.text: Jamm, at the hearing, says he's 'a big fan of your writing' to Donna, who is being called to testify about sending a sexual tweet.
jokes.setup: Jamm calls Donna to testify at the hearing about her explicit tweet.
jokes.punchline: He opens by telling her he's a fan of her writing — treating her explicit personal tweets as a literary body of work.
jokes.explanation: A sharp double-meaning joke. Calling Donna's sexual tweets 'writing' and expressing fandom is both creepy and funny. Jamm's sleaziness is consistent with character and the formal hearing context makes it land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You need to fill out Form 27-B to proceed with your request.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.line: What's Form 27-B?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's the application for hangar space at the regional airport.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.line: But I'm not trying to store a plane.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, you should've thought of that before you decided to exist in Pawnee.

jokes.text: Donna calls out a double standard: Councilman Dexhart is currently being sued for sexual harassment by two women, one of whom was the judge in the first woman's trial.
jokes.setup: Donna is on the defensive about her tweet being treated as a scandal.
jokes.punchline: She points to Dexhart's harassment case — which is being simultaneously prosecuted by a woman who is also suing him — an absurd recursive legal situation.
jokes.explanation: A structurally brilliant joke. The revelation that the judge in Dexhart's harassment case is ALSO suing him for harassment is a logically escalating absurdity that rewards a moment's thought. It's also sharp political satire about selective outrage. The economy is excellent — it lands the full absurdity efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Is that... are those party supplies in aisle seven? I think I see streamers. We should probably check on those immediately. For safety reasons.

jokes.text: Dexhart's explanation: 'She was talking dirty to me.' / Leslie: 'She was reading the emails that you sent to the first woman.'
jokes.setup: Dexhart tries to defend himself from the judge-also-suing-him revelation.
jokes.punchline: His defense — 'she was talking dirty to me' — is immediately demolished: she was reading his own harassment emails aloud as evidence.
jokes.explanation: The perfect punchline to joke #47. The idea that Dexhart's emails were so explicit that having them read aloud in court constitutes 'talking dirty to him' is a brilliant layered joke. It simultaneously indicts Dexhart's writing, his perception, and his complete lack of self-awareness. Structure is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: News reporter
dialogue.line: We've obtained access to a private Twitter account through a third party.

dialogue.speaker: News reporter
dialogue.line: That third party is our shared hairdresser.

jokes.text: Donna's hairdresser leaked her private tweets. 'Damn it, Typhoon! Why'd you do this?' / 'Maybe if you had bothered to come to my Great Gatsby Brunch, you'd know.'
jokes.setup: It's revealed that Donna's private tweets were obtained via 'a third party.'
jokes.punchline: The third party is Typhoon, her hairdresser, who leaked them in revenge for Donna skipping his Great Gatsby Brunch — a gloriously petty and specific motivation.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The reveal of the hairdresser leak is funny enough, but 'maybe if you had come to my Great Gatsby Brunch, you'd know' is spectacular. The specificity of 'Great Gatsby Brunch' as the grievance, the petty social revenge motivating a formal government hearing scandal, and the deadpan delivery all combine for a near-perfect joke. 'Great Gatsby Brunch' alone is brilliant. Justifies the 8+ score clearly.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: You told everyone at the community center about my bunions?

dialogue.speaker: Hairdresser
dialogue.line: That's right. And you know why? Because you didn't come to my themed brunch party.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: A themed brunch?

dialogue.speaker: Hairdresser
dialogue.line: It was Mimosas and Memes. You broke my heart, Donna.

jokes.text: Ron's reaction to the ballpark figure of his wealth: 'Holy fuck. / Is this a joke?' / Ron (re: jokes): 'Another word for jokes is lies. I do not lie. Therefore, I do not joke.'
jokes.setup: Ron reluctantly gives a ballpark figure for his wealth. The lawyer is shocked by the number.
jokes.punchline: The lawyer's 'Holy fuck' implies the fortune is staggeringly large. Ron's response to being asked if it's a joke — 'Another word for jokes is lies. I do not lie. Therefore I do not joke' — is a perfect syllogism of Swanson philosophy.
jokes.explanation: Multiple excellent beats stacked here. The lawyer's uncontrolled reaction to Ron's wealth is funny. But the killer is Ron's philosophical statement about jokes: it's structured as a logical syllogism, it perfectly encapsulates his entire character (literal, humorless, principled), and it's delivered with total sincerity. 'Another word for jokes is lies' is an all-time Ron Swanson line and easily justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: According to these documents, your net worth is... Holy shit.

jokes.text: Donna to Typhoon: 'Damn it, Typhoon! Why'd you do this?' / Typhoon: 'Maybe if you had bothered to come to my Great Gatsby Brunch, you'd know.'
jokes.setup: Donna confronts Typhoon about leaking her tweets.
jokes.punchline: Typhoon's response implies not only was the brunch snub the motivation, but that coming to the brunch would have somehow EXPLAINED why he'd leak tweets — a logic that doesn't hold up but is delivered with complete indignant confidence.
jokes.explanation: Typhoon's line has a great internal absurdist logic: attending the brunch would somehow explain the leaking? The wounded dignity of the delivery makes this land. 'You'd know' implies causality that isn't there, which is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Trevor
dialogue.line: You're telling me you have three million dollars?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's correct.

dialogue.speaker: Trevor
dialogue.line: How is that possible?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't spend money on frivolous things. I don't go to restaurants, I don't take vacations, I don't own a computer. I just work and save. It's a very simple philosophy.

dialogue.speaker: Trevor
dialogue.line: Well, that's... that's actually very impressive.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Also, jokes are lies told in a social setting. I don't tell jokes, so people assume I'm very wealthy. I am.

jokes.text: Ben attempts an emotional 'confronting your own mortality' speech to Ron. Ron listens patiently, says 'I had not considered that... I think you may be on to something.' Then: 'Oh, you're joking.' Ron: 'Yes, son, I am. First joke ever. Don't care for it.'
jokes.setup: Ben gives an earnest psychological explanation for Ron's difficult behavior about the will.
jokes.punchline: Ron pretends to be moved and vulnerable, letting Ben believe he broke through — then reveals it was his first joke. His immediate verdict: 'Don't care for it.'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional bit. Ben's therapeutic monologue is set up as sincere and the moment where Ron seems moved is perfectly played. The reveal that it was Ron's first-ever joke is hilarious on its own. But 'Don't care for it' — his immediate one-sentence review of the concept of joking — is the best line. It callbacks joke #50's philosophy perfectly: he tried it, confirmed he doesn't like it, and will not be doing it again. The structure is impeccable. This is comfortably one of the episode's top three jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're a public servant, but you serve the public poorly. I've seen more competence in a sloth sanctuary. Now get out of my office.

jokes.text: Donna's tweet: 'Annoying-ass Leslie has given me another annoying-ass task. [stickers] [bitchboss hashtag]'
jokes.setup: The hearing enters Donna's private tweets about Leslie into the record.
jokes.punchline: The tweet about the sticker task — using Leslie's sticker strategy as the exact point of complaint — is a callback that contextualizes all the earlier sticker comedy as a known Donna grievance.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the sticker plan makes this land harder — we've seen the absurd task that generated this tweet. The '#bitchboss' vs '#bossbitch' distinction set up later is seeded here. Good structural setup.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Leslie Knope is incompetent and her ideas are terrible. #ParksAndRec #DonnaKnowsBest

jokes.text: Donna's tweet about Leslie read aloud: '♪stickers, ♪bitchboss' / 'On a scale of 98 to 100, how annoying is Leslie Knope? Cuz u know it ain't less than 98.'
jokes.setup: Jamm enters Donna's private tweets into the public record at the hearing.
jokes.punchline: The tweets reveal Donna's genuine exasperation with Leslie — combining the sticker callback with a Twitter poll where the minimum rating is 98/100 annoying.
jokes.explanation: Strong cringe-comedy moment. The scale of '98 to 100' — where the minimum is already 98 — is a very funny construction. Callbacking the stickers while also landing in a genuine moment of workplace grievance makes this work on multiple levels.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A poll? About me? What are the options?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: 98% annoying, 99% annoying, or 100% annoying. Also, you're basically Sookie Stackhouse but less useful.

jokes.text: Leslie to Donna: 'That's what you really think of me? You think I'm annoying?' / Donna: 'Leslie, sometimes you're kind of annoying. I mean, I thought that was your thing.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is genuinely hurt by Donna's private tweets being made public.
jokes.punchline: Donna defuses with casual honesty — and the inadvertent cruelty of 'I thought that was your thing' implies everyone has accepted Leslie's annoyingness as a defining trait.
jokes.explanation: Good character-comedy beat. 'I thought that was your thing' is a casually devastating line — it's not mean-spirited but accidentally implies the whole office has categorized Leslie this way. Donna's unflinching honesty is a core character trait deployed well here.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'm not annoying. Annoying is your thing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No it's not!

jokes.text: Leslie: 'My thing is not being annoying. My things are making friendship bracelets and dancing like nobody's watching, thinking up really cool nicknames for my friends. You of all people should know that, El Diablo!'
jokes.setup: Leslie defends herself against the accusation that being annoying is 'her thing.'
jokes.punchline: Her list of 'things' — friendship bracelets, dancing like nobody's watching — is sweetly over-earnest, then punctuated by calling Donna 'El Diablo,' which undermines the wholesome list perfectly.
jokes.explanation: A very strong Leslie Knope character joke. The list of earnest 'things' is pure Leslie, and 'El Diablo' as the nickname she delivers with total sincerity while making a point about how nice she is is a perfect self-undermining punchline. It's also funny that she thinks El Diablo is a 'cool nickname' without any irony.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: My things are community organizing, local government, and breakfast foods. I'm passionate about these things.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Leslie, those are just regular things.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, they're MY things. Like, I organized the Harvest Festival, I got the Rededication of the Pit off the ground, I invented the concept of 'Treat Yo Self' day—

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: You didn't invent that.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, not invent, but I perfected it. And waffles, Donna. Waffles are my thing. I've had waffles for breakfast for the past 2,000 days straight.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: That's not a personality trait, that's a cry for help.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're just jealous because your thing is being mean, and nobody wants that thing, Saucy Mama.

jokes.text: Donna confessional: 'The only reason I'm even on Twitter is to blow off steam about work and tweet nasty stuff to dudes with washboard abs.'
jokes.setup: Donna addresses the severity of the situation.
jokes.punchline: Donna describes her Twitter use as having exactly two purposes: venting about work and flirting with abs. No other uses. Pure Donna economy of purpose.
jokes.explanation: A clean Donna confessional. The two-use framework for Twitter is funny for its reductive specificity. 'Washboard abs' is the right level of specific. High character integration — this is Donna's whole deal in one sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Leslie's management style is really quite effective. She leads with passion and optimism, which creates a positive work environment. She empowers her team members to take ownership of their projects, and she has this infectious enthusiasm that makes people want to work harder. She's also very detail-oriented and follows up on everything. I've been doing a lot of CrossFit lately, by the way. I'm up to 47 pull-ups in a single set. I also recently discovered this organic quinoa blend that has completely changed my approach to macronutrient distribution, and I'm only eating foods with a pH level above 7.

jokes.text: Leslie asks Ben five rapid-fire questions about whether he thinks she's annoying, ending with 'Do you think I'm being annoying right now?' / Ben: 'Yes.' / Leslie: 'So you DO think I'm annoying.'
jokes.setup: Leslie wants reassurance from Ben that she's not annoying.
jokes.punchline: She immediately demonstrates the annoyingness in question through the interrogation itself, and Ben's honest 'Yes' to the immediate question gets twisted into a confirmation of the broader accusation.
jokes.explanation: A self-referential structural comedy gem. Leslie's rapid-fire questions ARE the evidence. Ben's truthful answer to 'are you being annoying right now' — yes — gets conscripted into proving the larger point. The logic trap is beautifully constructed and character-perfect for both of them.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You know, Donna, the way you use hashtags is fascinating from a linguistic standpoint. It's almost like you're creating your own dialect.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I know what I'm doing, Chris.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm sure you do, but it's like... language is a lot like racquetball. You've got your walls, your angles, your velocity. And hashtags are the ball. You're just whacking them around with no regard for court positioning or basic strategy.

jokes.text: Ben: 'I like thinking.' / Leslie: 'And racquetball.' / Ben: 'Now who's annoying?'
jokes.setup: Ben gives a thoughtful speech about Leslie and ends with 'I like thinking.'
jokes.punchline: Leslie adds 'and racquetball' — a non-sequitur detail she's apparently filed away about Ben — and Ben turns the annoyingness accusation back on her.
jokes.explanation: A nicely executed short exchange. Leslie's ability to recall 'and racquetball' mid-serious conversation is a great character quirk — she files irrelevant details. Ben's flip of the annoying accusation is a satisfying button.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What's your airline called?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's called Jet Blue Ivy. It's a combination of Jet Blue and Blue Ivy Carter. And I'm predicting right now that we're gonna have a really good year.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'And racquetball.' Ben: 'And racquetball.' Leslie: 'Now who's annoying?'
jokes.setup: Ben adds 'And racquetball' to a sincere speech as a deflecting non-sequitur.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately calls him out: 'Now who's annoying?' — turning Ben's deflection into evidence for her own defense.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect callback payoff. Leslie's 'Now who's annoying?' completes the entire annoying-theme arc of the scene. It's also a winning character beat for Leslie — she wins the argument through Ben's own silliness. The economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I may have made a tiny adjustment to your permit application. But I have a solution. How about instead of a park, we spend some quality time together? I'm thinking dinner, maybe some wine, I'll wear my good jeans.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.line: Tom, you sabotaged my permit?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Sabotaged is such a strong word. I prefer 'strategically redirected.' But yes, now you're free to spend time with me instead.

jokes.text: Ben reveals more Donna tweets that are actually supportive of Leslie: '#bossbitch' vs '#bitchboss' distinction — 'It appears, whereas bitch boss is clearly an indication of frustration, boss bitch is a term of endearment. Isn't language fun?'
jokes.setup: Ben has found pro-Leslie tweets from Donna to balance the negative ones read at the hearing.
jokes.punchline: The entire dramatic emotional arc hinges on whether the order of 'bitch' and 'boss' is reversed — 'bitch boss' = insult, 'boss bitch' = compliment. Ben's 'Isn't language fun?' is the perfect scholarly punctuation.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed episode-level callback. The show sets up 'bitch boss' as damning, then resolves the Leslie/Donna tension by parsing the difference between two-word permutations. 'Isn't language fun?' delivered in Ben's nerd-with-genuine-enthusiasm register is the perfect cap. The joke works both as wordplay and emotional resolution, which is rare and excellent craft.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.line: I've been trying to get this permit for three months. Three months! I have a medical degree. I know diseases. And right now, I wish every single one of you government workers would catch the flu.

jokes.text: Donna's positive tweets about Leslie: '#bossbitch' vs. the earlier '#bitchboss' — 'It appears, whereas bitch boss is clearly an indication of frustration, boss bitch is a term of endearment. Isn't language fun?'
jokes.setup: Ben reads out more of Donna's tweets about Leslie, including supportive ones.
jokes.punchline: The distinction between 'bitchboss' and 'bossbitch' — and Ben's earnest linguistic analysis of the difference — is funny both as word play and as character comedy (very Ben to analyze this academically).
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed callback and wordplay joke. The reversal of word order carrying opposite emotional charges is genuinely clever linguistics, made funnier by Ben delivering it with academic earnestness. 'Isn't language fun?' is an excellent button. The follow-up 'It's like racquetball for your mouth!' is a great callback to the earlier racquetball joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I was just messing with you. Emotions are stupid.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ron, you can't reject the entire concept of human emotion.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Watch me.

jokes.text: Ben: 'It's like racquetball for your mouth!'
jokes.setup: Ben just said 'Isn't language fun?'
jokes.punchline: He extends the thought with an analogy to racquetball — his hobby — callbacking the earlier racquetball joke.
jokes.explanation: A fast, tight callback that works because it's unexpected — Ben's enthusiasm for language gets expressed through his enthusiasm for his weird hobby. The double callback in one beat (racquetball + language = 'racquetball for your mouth') is efficient comedy writing.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't believe in coddling my children. I give them a small allowance—five dollars a week—which teaches them the value of money while ensuring they never have enough to buy anything fun.

jokes.text: Nadia notices Tom has changed outfits. April (confessional): 'I changed five times, and she hasn't noticed yet.'
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to impress Nadia at the permit office.
jokes.punchline: Tom has apparently been changing clothes multiple times to find the right look; this has gone unnoticed by Nadia throughout.
jokes.explanation: April's deadpan confessional about Tom's futile outfit changes is a good visual-gag beat. The 'she hasn't noticed yet' undercuts the effort beautifully. Rewatch bonus since attentive viewers may catch outfit changes in earlier scenes.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have killed a boar. I have been killed by a boar. It's an endless cycle.

jokes.text: Tom has changed his outfit five times and Nadia hasn't noticed yet.
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to impress Nadia through clothing changes.
jokes.punchline: He has changed five times in the background of scenes and Nadia has been completely oblivious — establishing both his effort and its total irrelevance.
jokes.explanation: A good visual gag that rewards rewatchers who catch the outfit changes. The confessional delivery ('I changed five times') is the confirmation payoff. Tom's dedication to appearance vs. Nadia's complete indifference is a nice comedic contrast.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, hold on. 5% of Ron's fortune?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's like... that's still millions of dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ron, you can't give kids millions of dollars.

jokes.text: Tom filled out the wrong form again. 'I didn't know what to put for Name of Commercial Airline, because I do not operate a commercial airline, so I just made one up.'
jokes.setup: Tom is still using bureaucratic incompetence to stall Nadia.
jokes.punchline: Nadia has filled out what she thought was the right form and named a fictional airline for the field she couldn't answer — accepting the absurdity as the world's fault rather than Tom's.
jokes.explanation: Good continuation of the bureaucratic incompetence gag. Nadia's pragmatic response — just making up an airline name — is funny in how it validates the absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're naming me as guardian for your kids?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Actually, my first choice is the maitre d' at the steakhouse.

jokes.text: The fake airline is named 'Jet Blue Ivy.' 'I figure Jay-Z and Beyonce's kid will own her own airline eventually. She's the one.'
jokes.setup: Nadia made up a name for the commercial airline she doesn't own.
jokes.punchline: She named it after Blue Ivy, Jay-Z and Beyoncé's daughter, with the sincere logic that Blue Ivy will probably own an airline someday.
jokes.explanation: A very funny pop-culture gag. The wordplay on 'JetBlue' + 'Blue Ivy' is clean. But the joke's real charm is Nadia's sincere certainty that Blue Ivy is destined for airline ownership — and delivering this with 'She's the one.' It's absurdist but grounded in a real observation about celebrity wealth.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're just scoring cheap political points.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Cheap? These points are expensive. I have a very high-priced consultant who helps me score them.

jokes.text: Nadia: 'You said that park was ours. You said it a long time ago, in a British accent.'
jokes.setup: Tom says the park is no longer available.
jokes.punchline: Nadia's protest invokes the British accent — simultaneously the most and least credible thing about the original promise.
jokes.explanation: A good callback. 'In a British accent' as the detail Nadia chooses to cite in her grievance — as if the accent lent authority — is a subtle, well-earned joke.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Tom didn't sabotage anything. He's too incompetent to pull off sabotage. He can barely sabotage his own life.

jokes.text: Nadia: 'I probably shouldn't say this, as a doctor. But I really hope you all get West Nile virus.'
jokes.setup: Nadia is fed up with the incompetence of the Parks Department.
jokes.punchline: Her Hippocratic-oath violation — hoping everyone gets West Nile as a farewell — callbacks the earlier West Nile joke while being darkly funny.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed dark joke. A doctor professionally wishing disease on people is inherently funny. The setup — 'I probably shouldn't say this, as a doctor' — is a perfect self-aware frame. The West Nile callback ties it to the episode's mythology nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.line: You know what? Your desperate weirdness... I'm going to count that as romantic.

jokes.text: Ron: 'That has never been true.' — responding to Ben's 'We need to talk.'
jokes.setup: Ben approaches Ron with 'We need to talk.'
jokes.punchline: Ron's immediate refutation — 'That has never been true' — is a perfect encapsulation of his social philosophy (conversation is rarely necessary or welcome).
jokes.explanation: A four-word perfect joke. 'That has never been true' as a response to 'we need to talk' is extremely Ron — dismissing not just this conversation but the entire category of necessary conversations. It's immediately applicable to real life, highly quotable, and 100% character-specific. Justifies the 8+ score clearly.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Tom is an idiot. But he's OUR idiot. And he's going to mess things up, but he'll do it with the best intentions and a weird smile on his face. So yeah, he's terrible. But he's also kind of great.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I will leave my children $50 apiece for the cab home from my funeral and a steak dinner, end of discussion.'
jokes.setup: The lawyer and Ben are pressing Ron about how much to leave his children.
jokes.punchline: Ron's inheritance plan — $50 for a cab home and a steak dinner — is both extremely specific and extremely Ron: practical, meat-focused, and utterly without sentimentality.
jokes.explanation: A standout Ron Swanson joke that is highly specific and perfectly character-integrated. The idea of leaving your children just enough for a cab and a steak after your funeral — no more, no less — is quintessential Ron. 'End of discussion' seals it with his characteristic finality. The steak detail is particularly brilliant: he's thinking about their comfort but can't resist making it about meat. Easily justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Ben: 'If you want your kids to be left alone with no safety net just so they can learn some kind of weird lesson, then by all means, leave your fortune to the wild boar who gores you to death.'
jokes.setup: Ben is pushing back on Ron's plan to leave his kids almost nothing.
jokes.punchline: Ben invokes the killer-will premise — imagining the specific scenario of Ron being gored by a boar — as a reductio ad absurdum that inadvertently aligns perfectly with Ron's actual stated wishes.
jokes.explanation: A superb callback. Ben uses 'the boar who gores you to death' as hyperbole, not realizing it's literally Ron's plan. The specificity of 'gores' rather than just 'kills' shows Ben's mind has been shaped by Ron. And Ron's response ('I'd never lose to a boar') confirms he's thought about this scenario seriously. A well-earned escalation of the killer-will theme.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I'd never lose to a boar.'
jokes.setup: Ben suggests Ron might be gored to death by a wild boar.
jokes.punchline: Ron's response isn't 'that's absurd' but rather a confident, specific rebuttal about his ability to defeat boars — treating the scenario as entirely plausible but incorrectly forecasted.
jokes.explanation: A perfect four-word joke. Ron doesn't deny the scenario's possibility — he denies the outcome. His absolute confidence in his ability to defeat wild boars is both hilarious and completely in character. It also retroactively reframes the entire killer-will setup: Ron isn't pessimistic about dying, he simply hasn't identified a plausible killer yet. Economy is near-perfect. Justifies 8+ easily.

jokes.text: Leslie's apology gift: all of Donna's favorite lipsticks and nail polishes, with a printed schedule for wearing them at the same time. Leslie wants Donna to open each one in front of her and tell her how she feels about them 'individually.'
jokes.setup: Leslie gives Donna an apology gift to repair their friendship.
jokes.punchline: The gift has a printed coordination schedule, and Leslie wants individual emotional feedback on each item — a wildly over-structured approach to a reconciliation gift.
jokes.explanation: A good Leslie joke. The apology gift that comes with a PRINTED SCHEDULE for synchronized cosmetics wearing is pure Leslie Knope: her love is genuine but always overdone and slightly controlling. The 'tell me how you feel about them individually' is the perfect over-ask.

jokes.text: Donna: 'What's the hashtag gonna be? Boss bitch or bitch boss?' / Leslie: 'Yeah, it's psycho boss.' / Donna: 'Eh, I don't hate that.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Donna are taking a photo for Twitter after reconciling.
jokes.punchline: Leslie suggests '#psychoboss' as the hashtag — a self-deprecating upgrade on Donna's previous unflattering tags — and Donna grudgingly endorses it.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback button. Leslie's self-aware embrace of '#psychoboss' shows she's processed the episode's lesson. Donna's 'Eh, I don't hate that' is the minimum viable endorsement — very Donna.

jokes.text: Ron tells Ben he's decided to leave each of his children 5% of his fortune. Ben: 'Wow, 5 whole percent.' Then Ben and the lawyer realize 5% of Ron's hidden fortune is an enormous amount.
jokes.setup: After all the debate about leaving children nothing, Ron announces 5% each — which initially sounds small.
jokes.punchline: The lawyer's visible shock ('Holy fuck' callback implied) and Ben's realization ('Oh my God, that's 5%? That is a lot of money') reveal that 5% of Ron's hidden wealth is staggering.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed misdirection. '5 whole percent' sounds like a punchline to a bad-dad joke, but the reversal — where 5% is actually a fortune — subverts it elegantly. It also resolves Ron's character arc (he DOES love his kids) while maintaining his stoic exterior. The structural payoff is very well-earned.

jokes.text: Ron reveals he's leaving each child 5% of his fortune. Ben: 'Wow, 5 whole percent.' Ron: 'Oh my God, that's 5%? That is a lot of money.'
jokes.setup: Ben expects Ron to be stingy (following the $50 plan). Ron announces 5%.
jokes.punchline: Ben's sarcastic 'Wow, 5 whole percent' is undercut when the reveal of Ron's fortune means 5% is apparently a staggering sum. Ron's 'That is a lot of money' shifts the joke from Ron being stingy to Ron being obscenely wealthy.
jokes.explanation: A great structural callback. Ben's dismissive reaction ('5 whole percent') sets up as a Ron-is-stingy joke, then is immediately subverted when we realize 5% of Ron's fortune is apparently jaw-dropping. The misdirect works because Ben played it straight and the reversal reveals Ron's wealth through reaction rather than number-stating.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Wait, is this a joke?' / Trevor: 'It is not a joke. Not that an accountant would know the difference.'
jokes.setup: Ben and the lawyer react to the 5% revelation.
jokes.punchline: Trevor gets a dig in at Ben's accountant joke-making history — 'not that an accountant would know the difference' — a clean callback to the entire pun subplot.
jokes.explanation: A well-placed closing callback to the accountant/puns subplot. Trevor's dig — 'not that an accountant would know the difference' — is a good button, implying Ben's jokes were so bad they've permanently damaged Trevor's faith in accountants' judgment.

jokes.text: Ron names Ralph Piatkowski, the Maître D' at Mulligan's Steakhouse, and his wife Helen as guardians for his children — because Ralph 'knows him better than anyone.' Ben and Leslie are 'choice number two.'
jokes.setup: Ron is designating guardians for his children in case he and Diane die.
jokes.punchline: His first choice isn't family or close friends — it's a steakhouse maître d' — because food service has created the deepest bond Ron has with another human.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely brilliant character joke. The logic is internally consistent — of course Ron's deepest bond is with someone who feeds him well — but it's absurd by any normal standard. 'He knows me better than anyone' about a maître d' is the kind of insight into Ron's values that the best Ron jokes deliver. The 'as they're in their 90s, which seems likely' qualifier is a great deadpan acknowledgment that this is a bad plan.

jokes.text: Jamm: 'Everyone, take your seats, so this witch hunt may proceed as scheduled.' / Someone: 'Speaking of, where are the witches?' / The witch coven shows up to claim their park reservation.
jokes.setup: Jamm uses 'witch hunt' as a political metaphor in the hearing. Simultaneously, the witch coven from the episode's opening (the parks reservation policy) arrives.
jokes.punchline: Jamm's metaphorical 'witch hunt' is immediately taken literally as the actual witches show up — a perfectly constructed comedic coincidence.
jokes.explanation: An elegant structural callback. The 'witch hunt' metaphor colliding with actual witches is a well-constructed comedic payoff to the episode's opening absurdist premise. The timing of 'Speaking of, where are the witches?' makes it feel organic rather than forced. Good long-form comedic architecture.

jokes.text: The witches: 'We're not witches. That's sexist and offensive. But we're right here, and we are not gonna sit in this room and let you drag our names through the mud just to score some cheap political points.' / Jamm: 'How dare you demean the value of the political points I'm scoring?'
jokes.setup: The 'witch coven' stands up to defend themselves and Leslie.
jokes.punchline: Jamm's outrage isn't at being called out for cynicism — it's at having his political points 'demeaned.' He defends the value of his shameless political maneuvering with sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Jamm's response to being called out for scoring cheap political points — defending the VALUE of those points rather than denying the charge — is a perfect character joke. It reveals total shamelessness through the specific nature of his offense. Well-constructed and very quotable.

jokes.text: Jamm: 'Donna, quit punishing me! I miss you.' / Donna: 'Uh-uh! Bridge burned, Typhoon. Or should I say, Norman? Uh-huh.'
jokes.setup: Jamm calls out to Donna as she walks out, revealing an unexpected prior relationship.
jokes.punchline: Donna reveals Typhoon's real name is 'Norman' — an unglamorous secret she drops as a mic-drop exit line.
jokes.explanation: A great exit moment. The reveal that flamboyant hairdresser Typhoon is actually named Norman is perfectly timed as Donna's nuclear option. It implies a deep intimacy (she knows his real name) weaponized as a final devastating burn. The 'Uh-huh' button seals it.

jokes.text: Tom's new plan: 'Tell her all the screw-ups were your fault. I'll tell her I had to cover for you, because you are so dumb.' / April (to Nadia): 'Tom wants me to tell you that all the screw-ups were my fault, but really, he kept messing up so that you would stay in Pawnee as long as possible because he is super into you.'
jokes.setup: Tom finally decides to tell the truth about his feelings — except he chickens out and asks April to throw herself under the bus instead.
jokes.punchline: April immediately and completely blows up Tom's plan by telling Nadia the literal truth of what Tom asked her to lie about.
jokes.explanation: Excellently structured bit. Tom's elaborate new plan — which involves blaming April — is instantly and fully betrayed by April in the most direct way possible. April's non-explanation ('Tom wants me to tell you that... but really...') is completely April: she does the assignment while refusing to do the assignment. The structural payoff is satisfying because it reveals character for both Tom (cowardly romantic) and April (refuses to perform false loyalty).

jokes.text: Nadia: 'Is any part of him British?' / April: 'No.' / 'So, that was just weird, panicky dude behavior?' / 'Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Nadia is processing April's bombshell about Tom.
jokes.punchline: Nadia reduces Tom's elaborate fake-accent romantic strategy to 'weird, panicky dude behavior' — a perfectly accurate clinical summary.
jokes.explanation: 'Weird, panicky dude behavior' is a perfectly economical encapsulation of the episode's Tom subplot. April's flat 'Yeah' confirmation is the ideal straight-man beat. Great economy.

jokes.text: Nadia: 'I'm just trying to figure out if acting that insane is like, romantic, or totally scary.' / Tom: 'I'll go with romantic.'
jokes.setup: Nadia is processing that Tom faked a British accent and deliberately mishandled her paperwork out of infatuation.
jokes.punchline: Tom doesn't wait for Nadia to make the assessment — he answers for her, voting for the more flattering interpretation.
jokes.explanation: Tom's self-advocacy — choosing his own verdict in Nadia's rhetorical question — is a funny character beat. 'I'll go with romantic' is delivered with Tom's signature confidence. The moment is also sweet, which gives it a warmth that landing pure jokes sometimes lack.

jokes.text: April's pitch for Tom: 'He's sweet, he's cool, and you're, like, way out of his league, so there's literally no risk for you at all here.'
jokes.setup: Nadia is deciding whether Tom's behavior was romantic or scary.
jokes.punchline: April's romantic pitch on Tom's behalf includes explicitly admitting he's out of her league — framing it as a benefit to Nadia (no risk) rather than an insult to Tom.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully April-specific way to pitch someone for a date. She's technically trying to help Tom but frames it entirely in terms of Nadia's benefit — and 'way out of his league' is delivered as a selling point. Only April would sell someone this way, and it actually works.

jokes.text: Nadia: 'I am going to Rwanda in like two weeks for my job, so, what the hell?'
jokes.setup: Nadia is deciding whether to go on a date with Tom.
jokes.punchline: Her reasoning — she's leaving for Rwanda in two weeks, so why not — is both hilariously low-key and slightly insulting as a reason to date someone.
jokes.explanation: Funny deflation of the romantic setup — Nadia's reasoning is essentially 'I'm leaving soon anyway, so it doesn't matter.' A nice character joke that reveals she's cool but completely pragmatic.

jokes.text: April: 'Okay, you owe me, like, 1,000 favors. See ya.'
jokes.setup: April has just successfully gotten Nadia to agree to a date with Tom.
jokes.punchline: April's exit — 'you owe me 1,000 favors' — is delivered with complete casualness, as if this is just a transaction being logged.
jokes.explanation: A functional exit joke. The '1,000 favors' is a slight exaggeration that works because April delivers it completely dryly. Not exceptional but a clean button to the storyline.

tmdb_overview: Leslie throws Ben a birthday bash but is forced to leave early for an emergency late-night filibuster. Tom tries to make some memories with his new girlfriend, Ron and Donna go hunting. April reconnects with Andy.
insight: Deadpan delivery carries a mid-tier episode through 70 scattered jokes without standout punchlines.
